HUD counted 90 people in Posey County public housing in 2025
In 2025, HUD reported that public housing occupancy in Posey County, Indiana, reached 100%, with 83 available units.
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development counted 90 people living in Posey County, Indiana, public housing households that reported to the agency in 2025, spanning 83 households. This marked an increase of 2 from the 88 people reported in 2024.
Public housing occupancy stood at 100% in 2025, with all 83 available public housing units occupied. The occupancy rate remained unchanged from 100% in 2024.
On average, these reported households paid $435 per month toward rent and utilities, up from $386 per month in 2024. Their average annual household income was $23,193 in 2025, which increased from $22,259 in 2024.
The president's fiscal year 2027 budget request for the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development proposes $73.5 billion in gross discretionary funding, 13% less than the $84.2 billion enacted for fiscal 2026. The proposal includes about $38.9 billion for tenant-based rental assistance, which supports Housing Choice Vouchers, and $8.6 billion for the Public Housing Fund. It also proposes eliminating funding for the HOME Investment Partnerships Program and Community Development Block Grant program.
Public housing authorities face an estimated $170 billion backlog of repairs and other capital needs nationwide, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. In August 2026, HUD updated its guidance to make it easier for authorities to redevelop, sell or convert aging public housing properties, including through arrangements that can draw on private financing.
Housing costs strained nearly half of U.S. renter households in 2024. About 22.7 million households, or 49% of renters, spent more than 30% of their income on rent and utilities, according to the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies. Of those households, 12.1 million spent more than half their income on housing.
In May 2026, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development recommended that state and local governments streamline residential permitting and review zoning-board timelines. Its guidance also calls for faster permit reviews and clearer lists of the approvals required to build homes.
